title: Count Integers in Intervals
description: Brute force to optimized: tracking every individual integer versus merged, sorted intervals with an incrementally maintained running total count.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a data structure that stores intervals of integers via add(left, right), which adds every integer from left to right, inclusive, and supports count(), which returns the total number of distinct integers currently added across all intervals.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Added ranges can overlap, and each integer must only count once","Merge overlapping (or touching) ranges, exactly like Range Module"],["count() must be answered instantly, not recomputed from scratch","Maintain a running total alongside the merged intervals, updated incrementally on each add"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

This is Range Module's addRange operation, combined with a running count of distinct integers covered so far. Maintain a set of covered integers as merged intervals, and answer count() instantly at any time.

blocks.title: Analogy: Tracking Total Reserved Seats Across Merging Blocks
blocks.text: Picture reserving blocks of seats in a large venue, where overlapping or adjacent reservations merge into a single larger block, and needing to know the total number of currently reserved seats at any moment, without re-counting from scratch every time.

blocks.caption: Keep intervals merged and sorted; maintain a running total count alongside them

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: add(2,3), count(), add(7,10), count(), add(5,8), count()
After add(2,3): count is 2. After add(7,10): count is 2+4=6. After add(5,8): [5,8] merges with [7,10] into [5,10] (since 7,8 already counted, only 5,6 are new), giving a total of 8.
5. How Should We Think?
Before tracking every individual integer, notice this is exactly Range Module's addRange, with a running total count maintained alongside the merged interval list.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Storing covered integers as a sorted list of merged, non-overlapping intervals is compact regardless of how large the integer range is.

Observation 2: When add(left, right) is called, only the existing intervals that OVERLAP OR TOUCH [left, right] need to merge with it; everything else stays untouched.

Observation 3: Before merging, subtract the sizes of the intervals about to be replaced from the running total; after computing the new merged interval, add its size back in.

Observation 4: This keeps the running total always correct, letting count() be answered in O(1) at any time.

This leads to maintaining a sorted list of merged intervals (as in Range Module), together with a running total count, updated incrementally by subtracting replaced intervals' sizes and adding the new merged interval's size on every add.
6. Brute Force Solution
Track every individual integer added in a hash set; add(left, right) inserts every integer in the range, and count() returns the set's size.
Step by step algorithm

items: add(left, right): insert every integer from left to right into a set.
count(): return the size of the set.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every individual integer in a range is inserted directly, tracking coverage exactly.
With ranges up to 10^9 wide, this is completely impractical, both in time and memory.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(right minus left) per add, potentially up to 10^9.
Space: O(total distinct integers covered), potentially enormous.
Limitation: given ranges up to 10^9 wide, tracking individual integers is entirely infeasible; a merged-interval representation (as in Range Module) is required.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why tracking individual integers is unnecessary: covered integers naturally form contiguous merged ranges, exactly as in Range Module.

What additionally needs tracking here: a running total count of covered integers, updated incrementally rather than recomputed by summing every interval's size on each count() call.

How add() updates the total: before merging any overlapping/touching intervals into the new one, subtract their sizes from the running total; after computing the new merged interval's size, add it back in.

The core idea: maintain merged intervals like Range Module, plus a running total updated by exactly the size difference on every add, giving O(1) count() queries.

Maintain a sorted list of merged, non-overlapping intervals, and a running total. On add(left, right), find every existing interval overlapping or touching [left, right], subtract their sizes from the running total, merge them all with the new range into one interval, add its size to the running total, and replace them in the list. count() simply returns the running total.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for add(2,3), add(7,10), add(5,8)

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: merge intervals like Range Module, track a running total incrementally

codes.python:
class CountIntervals:
    def __init__(self):
        self.intervals = []           # sorted, merged, non-overlapping [left, right]
        self.total = 0

    def add(self, left, right):
        res = []
        i, n = 0, len(self.intervals)
        while i < n and self.intervals[i][1] < left - 1:
            res.append(self.intervals[i])
            i += 1
        new_left, new_right = left, right
        while i < n and self.intervals[i][0] <= right + 1:
            self.total -= self.intervals[i][1] - self.intervals[i][0] + 1   # remove the old size
            new_left = min(new_left, self.intervals[i][0])
            new_right = max(new_right, self.intervals[i][1])
            i += 1
        res.append([new_left, new_right])
        self.total += new_right - new_left + 1                              # add the new merged size
        res.extend(self.intervals[i:])
        self.intervals = res

    def count(self):
        return self.total

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since intervals are always kept merged and sorted, only a contiguous stretch of existing intervals can possibly overlap or touch a new [left, right]; subtracting exactly their combined size and adding back the new merged interval's size keeps the running total exactly correct at every step, since no integer is ever double-counted or missed. count() then answers instantly, since the total is maintained incrementally rather than recomputed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per add in the worst case (n being the current number of stored intervals), O(1) per count().
Space: O(n) for the stored intervals.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Count Integers in Intervals is Range Module's merging logic plus one added twist: maintaining a running total count incrementally, so it never needs to be recomputed from the interval list.
Common Mistakes

items: Recomputing the total by summing every interval's size on each count() call, instead of maintaining it incrementally.
Forgetting to subtract the OLD sizes of merged intervals before adding the NEW merged interval's size, causing double counting.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Recognizing this as Range Module with a maintained running total is the fastest path to a correct and efficient solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "does this remind you of another problem", think: this is Range Module's addRange, plus a running total count maintained incrementally.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support a removeRange operation as well, decrementing the total correctly?
How would you speed up finding the affected intervals using binary search instead of a linear scan?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs add in O(right - left) time. The optimized merged-interval approach runs add in O(n) time and count in O(1). Space is O(total covered integers) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: merged, sorted intervals (as in Range Module) with an incrementally maintained running total.
Core Idea: merge overlapping/touching intervals on each add, subtracting replaced intervals' sizes and adding the new merged size to a running total, so count() is always O(1).
Time: O(right - left) per add for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach; O(1) count() for the optimized approach.
Space: O(total covered integers) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: this is exactly Range Module, with a running total maintained alongside the merged intervals.
Interview Difficulty: straightforward once recognized as Range Module with an added running count.
One line memory trick: merge intervals like Range Module, track the total incrementally.
